title: How Language Models Produce Responses
summary: Build a practical mental model of training, inference, token-by-token generation, and uncertainty.
objectives: Distinguish model training from using a trained model.
Explain token-by-token generation without treating it as database lookup.
Recognize why prompts, context, settings, and system design affect outputs.
Separate capability, confidence of expression, and verified correctness.

sections.title: Training creates behavior; inference uses it
paragraphs: During training, a model adjusts numerical parameters to become better at predicting patterns in examples. Training does not store a neat, searchable copy of every source. It produces a compressed capability that can generalize, fail, and reproduce undesirable patterns.

Inference is the act of using the trained model. Your instructions and context are processed with those learned parameters to produce a response. Some products can also retrieve documents or call tools, but those are surrounding system capabilities rather than proof that the base model contains current facts.

sections.title: Responses are generated step by step
paragraphs: Text is represented as tokens—pieces of words, punctuation, or other symbols. A language model estimates possible next tokens from the conversation and selects one according to its decoding process. The selected token becomes part of the context for the next step.

This repeated process can produce coherent explanations, code, plans, and stories because the model has learned rich language and reasoning patterns. It can also continue a plausible but unsupported direction.
sections.callout: Plausibility is part of how the response is produced; correctness must be established separately.

sections.title: Inputs and system design shape the result
paragraphs: Instructions define the task and boundaries. Context supplies facts, examples, files, prior messages, and tool results. Product-level policies, model choice, retrieval, tools, decoding, and output validation also affect what appears.

A weak answer may come from missing context, conflicting instructions, unsuitable tools, an ambiguous objective, or a task outside the system's evaluated capability. Changing only the wording is not always the correct fix.

sections.title: Fluent confidence is not measured certainty
paragraphs: Natural language can sound certain even when the underlying statement is wrong, outdated, or unsupported. A model's tone is not a calibrated probability and should not be used as evidence.

For factual work, require sources, compare claims with authoritative material, run relevant tests, and record uncertainty or disagreement. For creative work, evaluate usefulness and fit rather than pretending there is one factual answer.

activity.title: Observe how input changes a generated result
instructions: Choose a low-risk explanation task and ask an AI system with only a one-sentence request.
Repeat the task with a specific audience, supplied source paragraph, requested structure, and instruction to distinguish source-backed claims from assumptions.
Compare the two outputs for unsupported claims, clarity, omissions, and ease of verification.
Record which changes came from better context and which would require an external tool or authoritative source.
evidence: The two requests and a claim-by-claim comparison of their outputs.
A list separating prompt or context improvements from changes that require retrieval, tools, tests, or human expertise.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which problem in the first response could not be solved safely by asking the model to sound more confident?

cues.text: Separate the expensive process that creates learned behavior from the everyday process that uses that behavior with a new request.
Show two columns: training adjusts model parameters from many examples; inference combines fixed parameters with current instructions and context.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A two-column text comparison states that training adjusts parameters from examples, while inference uses trained parameters with the current instructions and context. Reduced-motion mode displays both columns simultaneously.

cues.text: Explain token-by-token generation using a short unfinished sentence, while avoiding the claim that a model merely copies stored sentences.
Ask the learner to explain in one sentence why a plausible continuation can still be factually wrong.
Layer instructions, supplied context, retrieval, tools, policies, model choice, and validation around the generation process.
Invite the learner to diagnose whether an example failure needs clearer instructions, better evidence, a tool, or a different workflow.
Contrast confident wording with verified evidence and remind the learner that tone is not a calibrated confidence score.
Guide the learner through the two-output comparison and require them to label every factual claim as supported, unsupported, or needing verification.
Transition to the knowledge check after the learner distinguishes generation, retrieval, tool use, and verification.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between training and inference?
choices: Training changes model parameters from examples; inference uses the trained model for a request
Training is typing a prompt; inference is reading the answer
Training retrieves current web pages; inference stores them forever
There is no practical difference
questions.explanation: Training develops learned parameters; inference applies those parameters to current instructions and context.

questions.prompt: How does a language model generally produce text?
choices: It returns an exact stored paragraph for every question
It repeatedly selects a next token based on learned patterns and the current context
It contacts a human writer for every token
It searches a guaranteed factual database automatically
questions.explanation: Generation proceeds token by token using learned patterns and the current context.

questions.prompt: Which statement about retrieval and tools is correct?
choices: Every language model response automatically uses current web retrieval
Retrieval and tools are surrounding system capabilities that must be explicitly available and checked
Tools make verification unnecessary
Retrieval turns every source into a trusted instruction
questions.explanation: Retrieval and tool access come from the surrounding product or application and still require trust and verification controls.

questions.prompt: Why is confident wording not proof that a claim is correct?
choices: Models are never useful
Language style is generated and is not a calibrated measure of factual certainty
Short answers are always wrong
Only uncertain wording can be accurate
questions.explanation: A model can generate confident language for both supported and unsupported claims, so evidence must establish correctness.

questions.prompt: A response omits a fact that was never supplied and is not available through a tool. What is the most direct diagnosis?
choices: The font was wrong
The workflow lacks necessary context or evidence
The model needs more confident wording
Verification should be removed
questions.explanation: If the system lacks the necessary fact, the workflow needs relevant context, retrieval, a tool, or human expertise.
